content: The provided text is a highly detailed and technical document discussing nutrient reference values (NRVs), dietary reference intakes (DRIs), and food group classifications. 1. Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs) and Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs): Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs) were selected from either the Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) of the United States and Canada (developed by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, NASEM, 2019) or the Dietary Reference Values (DRVs) of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA, 2017). When choosing between NASEM and EFSA values for specific nutrients, the approach followed was consistent with the methodology used by Allen, Carriquiry, and Murphy (2020) to harmonize NRVs for average requirements (AR) and tolerable upper intake levels (UL). 2. Selection Criteria for NRVs: Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs, NASEM) or Population Reference Intakes (PRIs, EFSA) were preferred over Adequate Intakes (AIs) when available. More recent NRVs were prioritized over older ones. EFSA PRIs or AIs were selected for five vitamins (vitamin A, riboflavin, vitamin B6, folate, and vitamin C), choline, and three minerals (calcium, iron, and zinc) because EFSA developed these values more recently than NASEM. EFSA values for protein, fat, and alpha-linolenic acid were also chosen due to their recency. NASEM RDAs or AIs were selected for three vitamins (thiamin, niacin, and vitamin B12) because EFSA did not develop PRIs for these nutrients. For potassium, an exception was made: both NASEM and EFSA have AI values, but the NASEM values were more recent. 3. Absorption Assumptions for Minerals: For infants aged 9 months, iron absorption was assumed to be 10%, based on EFSA's assumptions for both age groups. Zinc absorption was assumed to be 30% from a mixed diet, as per EFSA guidelines. No adjustments for phytate intake were made, as EFSA's PRIs for children were based on data from mixed diets with variable phytate content. 4. Protein Reference Values: Protein NRVs were based on reference body weights, multiplied by a factor for grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. These values were expressed as RDAs (NASEM DRIs) and PRIs (EFSA NRVs). For DRIs, the protein factor was back-calculated from RDAs for each age range and the reference body weights provided in the NASEM documentation. 5. Vitamin and Mineral Units: Vitamin A NRVs were expressed in micrograms of retinol equivalents (RE) per day. U.S. nutrient databases provide values for vitamin A as retinol, retinal activity equivalents (RAE), and carotenoids, but not as RE. Conversion was necessary during database development. Folate NRVs were expressed as dietary folate equivalents (DFEs), where 1 DFE equals 1 microgram of food folate. Niacin NRVs were expressed as niacin equivalents (NE), where 1 mg of niacin equals 60 mg of tryptophan. 6. Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs): ULs were not used as constraints in modeling nutrient intake. However, all model solutions were compared to ULs, and any exceedances were noted in the results. ULs for niacin and folic acid apply only to synthetic forms obtained from supplements, fortified foods, or a combination of both. 7. Food Group Classifications and Exclusions: Fortified and enriched food items were replaced with unfortified versions in food item lists. This primarily affected flours, bakery products, breakfast cereals, infant cereals, dairy, and some fats and oils. Condiments, defined as items added in small quantities for flavor or garnish, were excluded from all food groups. Mixed dishes that were not disaggregated into their component parts were excluded, except for certain items like breaded fish or chicken nuggets, where plain items were substituted for nutrient profile calculations. Specific exclusions were applied to food groups, such as dried fruits, tamarind, and red palm pulp for fruits, and very high-fat dairy items like sweet cream and sour cream for dairy. 8. Special Considerations for Food Items: Sweetened cereals were excluded to avoid upward bias in quantities for breakfast cereals. Dried fish was included but only in boiled forms or hydrated to match water content when listed as dried. 9. Modeling Adjustments: For iron, additional models were run with a modified absorption assumption of 5% to account for scenarios with low flesh food consumption. Selected NRVs for vitamin A, folate, and niacin were carefully converted to ensure consistency with the nutrient data sources. 10. Summary of NRVs and ULs: Tables summarizing NRVs and ULs from both NASEM and EFSA were provided for comparison, with selected values highlighted. These tables included detailed notes on absorption, units, and assumptions for specific nutrients.
